## 2. Symbol Analysis

**1. The Spiritual Number 21:**

#### 2 + 1 = 3

In numerology, we often break down the number 21 of The World card into its components: 2 plus 1 equals 3. This actually reveals the process of transcendence from "duality" to "perfect creation."

Here, 2 represents duality and experience, much like the High Priestess, symbolizing everything we encounter on life’s journey—light and darkness, joy and sorrow, masculine and feminine. These seemingly opposing forces are actually necessary to form the wholeness of our life.

The 1 represents the individual and will, like the Magician, symbolizing the "self" that has integrated all experiences, an individual with complete consciousness and independent will.

3 corresponds to the Empress card, representing abundance, creation, and expression. The World card is essentially telling us: when you, as an independent individual, fully digest and absorb all dual experiences, a brand-new, creative state of life is born.

![Tarot illustration](https://internal-api-drive-stream.feishu.cn/space/api/box/stream/download/authcode/?code=MmFlOTMyMzg0MmFjOGM0ZjY4NDQ4ZTMxODNlOGY3MmJfMzM1MTU3ZjZlMmVkY2Q3ZmZhMzAzZGQ5YTZlNmMyOWRfSUQ6NzYyMzA4MjQ2MTcxNDUwMDgwNF8xNzgyMTgxNTA2OjE3ODIyNjc5MDZfVjM)

This is no longer just "having experience," but the ability to transform those experiences into wisdom, like the Empress, manifesting inner abundance and harmony into tangible success and joy. Simply put, this is "creation after integration." You no longer passively accept fate but become the master of your own life.

**2. Belongs to the Earth Element**

The World card belongs to the Earth element, but this does not refer to freshly turned soil; rather, it symbolizes stability, maturity, abundance, and sustainable reality. The Earth element itself represents the material world, wealth, the body, and all tangible results. The World card reveals the highest achievement possible when your spiritual pursuits and material practices perfectly combine. This is a truly "grounded" success, meaning your efforts and visions have transformed into visible, tangible reality. At the same time, Earth also symbolizes "stability" and "immovability." In The World card, this means you have established a solid inner and outer foundation. You no longer drift aimlessly but are as steady as the earth, able to firmly bear the abundance and joy of life.

**3. Astrological Correspondence: Saturn**

In astrology, The World card corresponds to Saturn, a planet representing limitation, responsibility, time, and ultimate achievement. Saturn’s core lessons revolve around structure, order, responsibility, and tests of time. The World card displays the highest accomplishment of Saturn’s energy—what is attained after long effort, rigorous trials, and relentless perseverance. It is not a stroke of luck but the inevitable result of "you reap what you sow." Although Saturn represents limitation, its ultimate purpose is to shape and accomplish through those limits. The World card means you have successfully mastered Saturn’s energy, transforming limitation into structure, pressure into motivation, and ultimately, through the refining of time, harvesting true freedom and maturity.

**4. Hebrew Letter: The Cross**

The Hebrew letter Tau (ת) means "cross." As the last letter of the alphabet, its shape resembles a cross. In the Kabbalistic system, this symbolizes "completion," "seal," and "mark of truth."

The horizontal axis of the cross represents the four directions (or four elements) of the material world, while the vertical axis represents the connection between spirit and matter. The dancer surrounded by the four elements (man, eagle, lion, ox) on The World card embodies this cross imagery. It symbolizes integrating all experiences of the material world within oneself, achieving perfect unity of spirit and matter. This also represents the "manifestation of truth." The truth you seek is no longer an abstract concept but has been "sealed" in reality through your life journey, becoming an achievement you can touch and feel. This card reminds you that you have completed your mission, and your life has left a unique "mark." Now, you stand at the end of a cycle, and this end itself is a perfect "sign," marking the complete conclusion of a stage.

## 3. Case Studies

Many people watching the ending of *Empresses in the Palace* (Zhen Huan Zhuan) feel that Zhen Huan is the ultimate winner. She personally sends the emperor away, supports her adopted son to ascend the throne, becomes the revered Empress Dowager, moves into the most prestigious palace, and holds the highest power in both the harem and the court. But if you look closely, this is not a simple victorious ending. Instead, it very much resembles the state of The World card in tarot—a stage of the journey has indeed come to a perfect close, but the overall cycle has not stopped. The old palace intrigues and grudges have ended, but a new round of power struggles has quietly begun behind the scenes.

When Zhen Huan first entered the palace, she was a naive young girl. Along the way, she experienced betrayal in love, lost her child, was marginalized to Ganlu Temple and suffered greatly, then gradually plotted revenge and finally climbed to the pinnacle of power. She defeated rivals like Hua Fei, the Empress, and An Lingrong, and even the emperor who once accompanied her became a target of her schemes. In the final episode, she stands outside the Yangxin Hall, her expression calm and indifferent, but her face no longer shows a genuine smile. She won every battle along the way but lost the most precious things—her youthful love, sincere friendships, and original innocence—all gone. At that moment, she completed her entire life’s cultivation, just like the dancer surrounded by the wreath of completion on The World card, having fully experienced everything and closed her own cycle.

The final scenes carry deep meaning. The newly crowned emperor is still young, the court situation unstable, and new women continue to enter the harem. Although Consort Jing and Consort Duan stand on her side, each has their own thoughts and positions. Even Shen Meizhuang’s daughter may become a pawn in the power game later. After Zhen Huan ascends to Empress Dowager, she appears to control everything but actually steps into a lonelier, more silent battlefield. The palace intrigues of the past had clear enemies; now, beneath the seemingly peaceful surface, everyone wears masks, and even her own children may not be fully trusted.

This is very much like The World card. It does not represent eternal victory and ending but the perfect completion of a stage and the subsequent transfer of identity and mission. Zhen Huan ended her old life of vying for favor, revenge, and power but naturally entered a new phase of maintaining, balancing, and stabilizing. The form of palace intrigue changed, but the desires deep in people’s hearts never did. She is no longer the concubine playing the game but the rule maker and guardian. Yet this guardianship itself is a longer, quieter contest.

Therefore, the ending of *Empresses in the Palace* is never a full stop but more like a brief pause—a comma. Zhen Huan becoming Empress Dowager seems to settle everything, but inside the Forbidden City’s red walls, a new round of tests, alliances, and undercurrents is quietly brewing. Like the endless cycle of seasons, when one ends, another naturally begins. Life never truly ends; it only completes one stage after another.

This is the truest nature of The World card. When you seriously finish a journey, you can pause to rest, look back, integrate all experiences, and celebrate your completion. But after a brief rest, new paths naturally appear beneath your feet. Zhen Huan sheds her former pearl hairpins and dons the Empress Dowager’s phoenix crown, her identity completely changed, but the battlefield remains. She has not exited the game called life but ascended to a higher-level table, where the game will continue forever.
